analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for them by removing the payroll tax cap and taxing large investment incomes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced June 29, 2026 with 3 cosponsors and referred to three House committees; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises Social Security benefits across the board, adopts a cost-of-living index that better reflects what older Americans buy, guarantees a minimum benefit tied to the poverty line for long-career low earners, credits years spent caring for children or dependent relatives, ends the 5-month wait for disability benefits, and extends child benefits to student dependents under 26. It pays for this by removing the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax, so all earnings are taxed, and by applying a 12.4% Social Security tax to investment income above $400,000. It also directs Social Security to rebuild its customer service staff and keep field offices open. Most of the benefit improvements take effect in 2027 and expire after 2036.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, disabled workers, and survivors receive larger checks; long-career low earners get a benefit floor set at the poverty line; unpaid caregivers of young children or chronically dependent relatives earn Social Security credit; disabled applicants get benefits about 5 months sooner; disabled beneficiaries who return to work no longer lose benefits abruptly; student dependents keep benefits through age 26; and beneficiaries with modest incomes pay less tax on their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, caregivers, low earners

how_it_helps.text: Raises the top benefit formula factor from 90% to 93%, increasing benefits across the board for 2027 through 2036.
Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment to whichever is higher — the standard wage-earner index or a new index tracking spending typical of people 62 and older.
Sets a minimum benefit for long-career workers that scales up to a percentage of the federal poverty guideline, reaching 125% of poverty for 30+ years of work.
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable to $35,000 for singles and $50,000 for couples.
Grants up to 5 years of deemed wages to unpaid caregivers of children under 12 or chronically dependent relatives.
Eliminates the 5-month waiting period before disability benefits begin.
Replaces benefit termination for disabled beneficiaries who return to work with a gradual $1-for-$2 reduction, so earning more never leaves someone worse off.
Extends child's benefits to dependents enrolled at least half-time in post-secondary school up to age 26, and eases eligibility for children living with grandparents or other relatives.
Improves survivor benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households and increases benefits for anyone on the rolls more than 15 years.
Directs Social Security to rebuild its customer service workforce and keep field offices open, and bars dual office-holding.

analysis.who_pays: High earners bear a 12.4% payroll tax on all wages with no annual cap (split with their employers), self-employed high earners bear it in full, and households with investment income above $400,000 pay an additional 12.4% Social Security tax on that income on top of the existing 3.8%.

drawbacks.text: Most benefit improvements are temporary: the across-the-board increase, the new COLA index, the minimum benefit, caregiver credits, the disability changes, and the child-benefit extensions all apply only to benefits for calendar years 2027 through 2036 and phase out after that.

Removing the wage cap and adding a 12.4% tax on investment income over $400,000 is a large tax increase on high earners and their employers; employers of high-wage workers pay the employer half of the tax on previously untaxed wages.

High earners would begin receiving some benefit credit on earnings above the current cap (at a 1% factor), but the value of that credit is far below the extra tax paid, which opponents say severs the link between contributions and benefits.
The bill merges the retirement, survivors, and disability trust funds into a single Social Security Trust Fund, a structural change that requires an extensive administrative transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly two-thirds of workers who earn under the current wage cap each year, this is close to a pure gain: larger, better-indexed benefits with no new tax. The cost falls almost entirely on the top slice of earners and on investment income above $400,000. The most serious design flaw is the 2036 sunset on the benefit improvements, which buys a decade of higher benefits without committing to fund them permanently — supporters would need to make the financing and the enhancements permanent to fully close Social Security's projected shortfall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2026 and sent to three committees — Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Energy and Commerce — and has sat without a hearing or vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson of Connecticut introduced the bill on June 29, 2026, and it was referred to the Ways and Means, Education and Workforce, and Energy and Commerce committees.
Three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committees have taken no action since referral — no markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet — the bill is simply sitting in committee with minimal sponsorship, so current beneficiaries and high earners are both in the same place as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — it sits in committee

for.name: Rep. John Larson (D-CT)
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act and referred it to three committees.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, but all four sponsors are Democrats and the bill sits with committees controlled by the 223-member House Republican majority, which has taken no action on it.

industries.note: The bill removes the annual cap on wages subject to the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax and adds a 12.4% tax on net investment income above $400,000. That is where the money to pay for higher benefits comes from.
Employers pay half of the FICA payroll tax on wages, so removing the cap means their payroll tax liability extends to every dollar of high salaries, not just the first capped amount.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries and their families
industries.note: The bill raises monthly checks, improves the COLA formula, adds caregiver credits, and speeds disability benefits for 2027 through 2036, with most provisions sunsetting after 2036.

analysis.trajectory: With four total sponsors, no committee action since referral, and a House agenda controlled by the Republican majority, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or vote this Congress. Versions of this proposal have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses without advancing; the realistic path is that it sits in committee until the session ends, unless its tax or benefit provisions get folded into a larger bipartisan Social Security package.
